title: Constructing a Low-budget Laser Axotomy System to Study Axon Regeneration in C. elegans
protocol: Wear laser safety goggles and use good laser safety practices during initial alignment.
Arrange components on the breadboard as shown in Fig. 1 (see also example2).
Bolt down the laser, periscope post, and elevated rail supports.
Position your microscope to align with the rail axis.
Align with the transmitted light beam from the microscope condenser lens.
Adjust the rail height using a level.
Align an adjustable aperture or lens at both ends of the rail to the condenser beam.
Secure the components to the breadboard.
Align the Glan-Thompson polarizer and half-wave plate to the laser beam.
Rotate the polarizer to provide a convenient orientation for the beam dump (fig.1).
Reduce power to a minimum using the half-wave plate.
Use a Post-It note or lens paper to visualize the laser beam.
Adjust the kinematically mounted mirrors sequentially from the laser.
Align the laser beam roughly to the center of the mirrors.
Orient the mirrors at approximately 45 degrees relative to the laser beam axis.
Coarsely adjust the kinematically mounted mirror on top of the periscope and rail.
Align the laser beam to the center of the transmitted light beam from the microscope using paper in the beam path.
Remove or fully open ND filters and apertures in the intermediate module.
Fine-tune the alignment of the laser beam to the center of the transmitted light beam with the fine adjustments on the top periscope and rail mirrors.
Hold a piece of paper close to the rail mirror and align the laser beam to the center of the transmitted light beam using the top periscope mirror.
Position a Post-It note in the beam path between the aligned condenser lens and open objective turret.
Align the laser beam near the center of the transmitted light beam with fine adjustments on the rail mirror.
Fix the microscope in place with clamps.
Turn off the laser.
Engage the mechanical safety shutter.
Rotate the 50% dichroic out of the beam path.
Mount the target slide for fine alignment and image with the 60X oil objective.
Focus on scratches on the slide.
Put in the ND4 and ND8 filter in intermediate module.
Image the target slide with your CLSM, Spinning disk, or CCD camera system.
Rotate the 50% dichroic into the laser path.
Set the mode to triggered, frequency to 100, and pulse number to 10.
Open the mechanical safety shutter.
Trigger the ablation laser while imaging the target slide.
Check for an ablation spot 1-10 μm in diameter on the target slide.
Sequentially remove ND filters until an ablation spot is seen.
Adjust the ablation spot to the center of the image using the rail mirror.
Add back a ND filter to have room to finely increase laser power with the half-wave plate for a <1 um ablation spot.
Image at 0.2 μm/pixel or less and finely adjust the ablation spot to the image center (position 256,256 with 512X512 image).
Check the depth of focus and axis of the laser beam.
Focus up and down 1-2 um and check the ablation position and ablation spot size.
If the laser beam is axially aligned, the ablation spot will not move.
Add lenses to expand the laser beam to fill the objective back aperture.
Adjust convergence to control focus using dual Galilean beam expanders.
Turn on the laser and adjust it to minimum power and continuous mode.
Roughly adjust the beam alignment through each lens using paper to see the laser beam and transmitted light beam from microscope condenser.
Turn off and shutter the laser.
Remove the clamps from one side of the microscope and slide the microscope out of the laser beam path.
Turn on the laser and remove safety shutter.
Perform fine alignment of the lenses and the laser beam by viewing the expanded laser beam on a nearby wall.
Adjust the last two kinematically mounted mirrors to align the beam.
Ensure the aligned and expanded beam profile is circular and uniform in brightness.
View the size and uniformity of the beam with a Post-It note at the estimated position of the objective back aperture.
Adjust the beam to zero convergence for infinity optical systems by noting how the beam size changes as you move a Post-It note farther from lenses.
Turn off the laser and engage the mechanical shutter.
Slide the microscope back into the laser beam path using the fixed clamps.
Replace the clamps on the free side of the microscope, but do not tighten them down.
Turn on the laser and remove the safety shutter.
Rotate the objective turret to an open position.
Place a Post-It note on the stage.
Center the expanded and uniform laser beam centered on the transmitted light beam from the condenser.
Loosen the microscope clamps if necessary to center the laser beam.
Engage the safety shutter, and set the laser to trigger mode.
Rotate the 60X objective in place and image the surface scratches on the target slide.
Remove the safety shutter, trigger the ablation laser, and adjust the laser power for the minimum ablation spot.
Center the ablation spot with fine adjustments of the kinematically mounted rail mirror.
Iteratively adjust the rail-mounted and top periscope mirrors to center the ablation spot while maintaining a uniform beam profile.
Evaluate the Z focus of the laser by moving the focus systematically up and down in 1 um steps and triggering the ablation laser.
Adjust the Z focus of the expanded beam by moving lens L3 of the Galilean telescope.
Reconstitute 10% Agarose in balanced saline until fully melted.
Keep the molten agarose on a hot plate during use for mounting.
Place a drop of molten agarose on a glass slide and flatten it with another glass slide into a pad approximately 200 μm thick using time tape as a spacer.
Cut out a uniform diameter circular pad of 13 mm.
Add 1 μl of Muscimol (20 mM) to the center of the agarose pad.
Add 1 μl of Polystyrene Microspheres (2.65%) to the center of the agarose pad.
Place 3-5 worms on their left sides in the center of the pad.
Apply a glass coverslip over the worms and agarose pad.
Seal the coverslip with Vaseline to prevent evaporation of the sample.
Align the laser to crosshairs at the beginning of each session.
Engage the laser safety shutter.
Remove the laser alignment target.
Image an adult worm mounted on the slide using a suitable fluorescent marker in the target neurons.
Image axons at a similar magnification (0.2 μm/pixel or higher) and position under the crosshairs.
Open the laser safety shutter.
Trigger the ablation laser while imaging.
Increase laser power until the axon is cut.
Set laser parameters to 100 pulses at 2.5 kHz with an average power of about 0.27 mW.
Cut the axon, observing a break of about 0.5-1 um without loss of brightness in the ends.
Equilibrate mounted worms with the microscope stage for 30 minutes before starting time lapse recording.
Monitor the proximal and distal axons to form retraction bulbs over the next 30 minutes.
Set up time-lapse imaging parameters using the associated imaging software.
Image 10-20 Z steps (1 um/step) at a resolution of 0.1-0.2 um/pixel.
Adjust gain, pinhole, scan rate, and imaging laser power to minimize exposure while achieving desired spatial resolution.
Sample images every 1-5 minutes over a period of 15 hours for temporal resolution.
Convert time-lapse image data into movies using NIS Elements or ImageJ software.
Remove the microscope clamps from one side of the microscope so the microscope can be moved out of beam path, but the remaining clamps will allow the microscope to be precisely repositioned.
Adjust the laser power to a minimum with the Glan-Thompson polarizer.
Turn on the laser and view the laser beam pattern on the wall.
Systematically adjust the positions of the lenses to get a feel for what they do to the beam size and appearance.
Use the rail-mounted mirror to adjust the intense spot to the center as shown in panel B.
Now use the top periscope mounted mirror to give a uniform peripheral profile.
Intercept the beam at the distance of the objective back aperture.
Evaluate convergence by comparing beam diameter at the distance of the objective back aperture and the wall.
Center the ablation spot and adjust the laser beam convergence for optimum focus.
Turn off and shutter the laser.
Remove the paper and mount the mirrored target slide.
Image scratches on the mirrored surface with the 60X 1.4na oil lens.
Image the surface with a confocal or CCD.
Set the laser to trigger mode, lowest power, and 100 Hz.
Trigger about 10 pulses.
Center the ablation spot to the field of view if necessary.
Put the cross hairs at 256, 256 coordinates if viewing 512X512 image.
Move the ablation spot to the center crosshairs using the rail mounted mirror.
Reevaluate the uniformity of the laser beam by looking at the beam with the objective removed.
Adjust the beam uniformity with the top periscope mounted mirror.
Evaluate the focus of the laser beam in the Z axis.
Trigger the laser to produce an ablation spot of about 1 um in the center.
Move the slide about 5 um laterally and focus 1 um below the surface of the target slide.
Focus 1 um above the surface of the target slide and trigger the laser using the same settings as for the first ablation spot.
Adjust lens L3 to align focal planes, making small adjustments near focus.
Cut axons after fine-tuning the focus.
Heat agarose 10% in saline until fully melted.
Place a small drop of the heated mixture on a glass microscope slide and flatten it with another slide to form a flat pad.
Allow the pad to set for about one minute.
Separate the slides after setting.
Use a "Sharpie" top as a cookie cutter to form a uniform-sized pad of approximately 13 mm.
Add 1 μl of 10 mM muscimol and 1 μl of microspheres to the center of the pad.
Place worms in the drop containing muscimol and microspheres, orienting them properly before placing on a glass coverslip.
Apply Vaseline from a syringe with a 20-25 gauge needle around the edge of the coverslip to seal it.
